hints: Imagine you have 100 g of V, so the percentages become masses in grams. Think about how to convert each mass to moles.
Once you have moles of C, H and O, consider how to get the simplest whole number ratio by using the smallest value.
Calculate the Mr of your simplest ratio and compare it with the given Mr of 280 to find the scaling factor.
walkthrough:
Turn percentages into moles**
Picture 100 g of V. You then have $77.2\text{ g}$ of $\text{C}$, $11.4\text{ g}$ of $\text{H}$ and $11.4\text{ g}$ of $\text{O}$. Divide each by its $A_{r}$ to get moles: $$n(\text{C}) = 77.2/12 = 6.433$$ $$n(\text{H}) = 11.4/1 = 11.4$$ $$n(\text{O}) = 11.4/16 = 0.7125$$ This tells you the relative number of atoms present.

Find the simplest whole number ratio**
Divide every value by the smallest, $0.7125$, to set oxygen to 1: $$\text{C} = 6.433/0.7125 = 9.03$$ $$\text{H} = 11.4/0.7125 = 16$$ $$\text{O} = 0.7125/0.7125 = 1$$ Round $9.03$ to $9$. The empirical formula is therefore $\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{16}\text{O}$.

Scale up to the true molecular formula**
Work out the mass of one empirical unit: $$M_{r}(\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{16}\text{O}) = (9 \times 12) + (16 \times 1) + 16 = 140$$ The real molecule has $M_{r} = 280$, which is twice as heavy: $$280/140 = 2$$ Multiply the empirical formula by 2 to get $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{32}\text{O}_{2}$.

Final answer: Moles: $C = 77.2/12 = 6.433$, $H = 11.4/1 = 11.4$, $O = 11.4/16 = 0.7125$
Ratio $\div$ smallest: $C:H:O = 9.03:16:1$, empirical formula $= C_{9}H_{16}O$
$Mr(C_{9}H_{16}O) = 140$, $280/140 = 2$, so molecular formula of V $= C_{18}H_{32}O_{2}$

hints: Recall which weak base reacts with acids stronger than carbonic acid to release a gas, but does not react with weaker acids like phenol or alcohols.
Think about what you would actually see if a colourless gas is rapidly evolved from a solution.
walkthrough:
Choose a reagent that only carboxylic acids will trigger**
Carboxylic acids are strong enough to react with a carbonate or hydrogencarbonate to release carbon dioxide. Alkenes, alcohols and most other neutral organics do nothing. A safe choice is sodium carbonate, $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$, or sodium hydrogencarbonate, $\text{NaHCO}_{3}$, either as solid or aqueous solution.

Link the chemistry to the observation**
The acid donates $\text{H}^{+}$ to the carbonate: $$2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ The $\text{CO}_{2}$ escapes as tiny bubbles, so you see brisk effervescence or fizzing. That bubbling confirms the $\text{COOH}$ group.

Final answer: Add $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ (or $\text{NaHCO}_{3}$) solution / solid.
Effervescence / fizzing / bubbling seen (due to $\text{CO}_{2}$).

hints: Calculate moles of $\text{Br}_{2}$ and moles of V separately using $n = m/M_{r}$, then remember one $\text{C=C}$ reacts with exactly one $\text{Br}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Compare moles to count the double bonds**
Each $\text{C=C}$ adds one $\text{Br}_{2}$ molecule across the double bond. Work out both moles: $$n(\text{Br}_{2}) = 3.196/159.8 = 0.0200\,\text{mol}$$ $$n(\text{V}) = 2.800/280 = 0.0100\,\text{mol}$$ The ratio is: $$0.0200/0.0100 = 2\,\text{mol Br}_{2} \text{ per mol V}$$ So one molecule of V must contain 2 alkene $\text{C=C}$ groups.
Final answer: $n(\text{Br}_{2}) = 3.196/159.8 = 0.02\,\text{mol}$, $n(\text{V}) = 2.800/280 = 0.01\,\text{mol}$, ratio $= 2:1$, so number of alkene groups in V $= 2$

hints: Recall what single reagent gives an orange precipitate with all three compounds W, X and Y.
walkthrough:
Read what the common positive test tells you**
All of W, X and Y give an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine. That reagent is specific for the $\text{C=O}$ group. So all three must contain the carbonyl functional group, with W and X later shown to be an aldehyde and a ketone respectively.
Final answer: carbonyl ($\text{C=O}$ / aldehyde and ketone)

hints: Recall the antiseptic smelling yellow solid formed in the positive iodoform reaction for methyl ketones.
walkthrough:
Name the yellow solid from alkaline iodine**
X gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}(\text{aq})$. This is the classic iodoform test for a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}$ group. The yellow solid is triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_{3}$.

hints: Use Table 4.1 to decide if W is an aldehyde or a ketone by comparing Fehling's and alkaline iodine results.
For formula $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ as an aldehyde, think how the $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}$ alkyl chain attached to CHO can be branched in different ways.
Recall the name for isomers that differ only in the branching of the carbon skeleton.
walkthrough:
Prove W must be an aldehyde**
W gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, so it has $\text{C=O}$. It gives an orange-red precipitate on warming with Fehling's reagent, which only aldehydes do among carbonyls, as the aldehyde is oxidised and $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is reduced to $\text{Cu}_{2}\text{O}$. It gives no change with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$, so it is not a methyl ketone. W is therefore a $\text{C}_{5}$ aldehyde, $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{CHO}$.

Draw two different carbon skeletons**
Keep the $\text{CHO}$ group at the end and rearrange the $\text{C}_{4}$ chain. Isomer 1, straight chain: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHO}$$ pentanal. Isomer 2, branched examples, any one of: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CHO}$$ 2-methylbutanal, or $$(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CHO}$$ 3-methylbutanal, or $$(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CCHO}$$ 2,2-dimethylpropanal. In skeletal form, draw zigzag carbon chains ending in the $\text{CHO}$ carbon, with methyl branches as short lines.

Name the isomer type**
All four possibilities have the same $\text{CHO}$ functional group in the same position at the end of the chain, only the arrangement of the carbon skeleton changes from straight to branched. This is chain isomerism, a type of structural isomerism.

Final answer: W is an aldehyde: e.g. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHO}$ [pentanal] plus any one other of: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CHO}$ [2-methylbutanal], $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CHO}$ [3-methylbutanal], $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CCHO}$ [2,2-dimethylpropanal] shown as skeletal formulae.
Type of structural isomerism: chain isomerism

hints: Check the small molecular ion peak at m/e 86 to confirm Mr, then think which simple alkyl fragment has mass 29.
For m/e 57, consider fragments containing C, H and O that add to 57, especially those formed by cleavage next to C=O in a ketone.
Combine the two fragments to rebuild a symmetrical or unsymmetrical C5 ketone that could split in that way.
walkthrough:
Assign the m/e 29 peak**
The molecular ion at $m/e = 86$ matches $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ ($60+10+16 = 86$). A fragment of mass 29 with only C and H is: $$12 \times 2 + 5 \times 1 = 29$$ so it is the ethyl cation, $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}^{+}$, formed by cleavage of an ethyl group from the ketone.

Assign the base peak at m/e 57**
Ketones commonly cleave next to the $\text{C=O}$ to give acylium ions. Mass 57 fits: $$12 + 16 + 29 = 57$$ for $\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}^{+}$, which is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C} \equiv \text{O}^{+}$. This is also written as $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{+}$. The alternative cleavage gives $\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{3}^{+}$, also mass 57. This is the base peak (100% abundance), showing this cleavage is very favourable.

Rebuild Z from its pieces**
If you see both $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}^{+}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}^{+}$, the molecule splits into two ethyl type pieces around the carbonyl: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$$ This is pentan-3-one, a symmetrical ketone. If the 57 fragment is viewed as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}^{+}$, the pieces rebuild to: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$$ pentan-2-one. Either deduction correctly matches the given fragments.

Final answer: $m/e = 29$: $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}^{+}$
$m/e = 57$: $\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}^{+}$ or $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{+}$ (accept $\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{3}^{+}$)
identity of Z: pentan-3-one, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ (if $\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}^{+}$) OR pentan-2-one, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ (if $\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{3}^{+}$)
